s: B. Article II powers and limits.
Vesting and Take Care.
"The executive Power shall be vested in a President."
Whether this clause grants power beyond the enumerated list is debated.
Unitary-executive scholars read it as a grant of all traditional executive power; others read it as a designation of office.
The President must "take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed," which implies both a duty to enforce and supervisory authority over subordinates.
Appointments.
Principal officers are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.
Congress may vest appointment of inferior officers in the President alone, the courts of law, or department heads.
An inferior officer is one directed and supervised by a principal officer (Edmond v. United States, 1997).

Officers are those exercising "significant authority pursuant to the laws of the United States" in a continuing position (Buckley v. Valeo, 1976; Lucia v. SEC, 2018, holding that SEC administrative law judges are officers).
If an inferior officer's decisions are not reviewable by a principal officer, that officer is effectively principal (United States v. Arthrex, 2021).
Recess appointments require a recess of at least ten days (NLRB v. Noel Canning, 2014).
Removal.
The Constitution is silent; doctrine has developed through the cases.
Myers v. United States (1926): the President may remove executive officers at will.
Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935): Congress may protect members of multimember expert agencies exercising "quasi-legislative" and "quasi-judicial" power from at-will removal.
Morrison v. Olson (1988): good-cause protection for an independent counsel, an inferior officer, upheld because it did not "impede the President's ability to perform his constitutional duty."
Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB (2010): two layers of for-cause protection are invalid.
Seila Law v. CFPB (2020) and Collins v. Yellen (2021): single-director independent agencies violate the separation of powers.
The current law treats at-will removal as the rule, with Humphrey's and Morrison as exceptions.
The scope of those exceptions is actively litigated, so check the current Term.
Foreign affairs and treaties.
The President makes treaties with the advice and consent of two-thirds of the Senate.
Executive agreements made without Senate consent are valid within the President's own powers or with statutory authorization (United States v. Belmont, 1937; Dames & Moore).
United States v. Curtiss-Wright (1936) described the President as "sole organ" of the nation in foreign relations; Zivotofsky II cautioned against reading that dictum broadly.
Non-self-executing treaties do not by themselves create domestic law enforceable in court (Medellín).
Pardons.
The pardon power covers "Offences against the United States" (federal crimes), not state crimes or impeachment.
It is otherwise broad, permitting conditional pardons and pardons before conviction (Ex parte Garland, 1866).
Commander in Chief and war powers.
Congress declares war.
The President may repel sudden attacks and directs the military once it is engaged.
The War Powers Resolution (1973) requires reporting within 48 hours and withdrawal within 60–90 days absent authorization; Presidents of both parties have contested its constitutionality.
Detention in wartime is subject to due process and habeas review (Hamdi v. Rumsfeld, 2004; Boumediene).
